entries.title: Poolease X1 Pool Robot Review: How Bad Can It Be?
entries.summary: The Poolease X1 can collect leaves from the pool floor, but dirt, silt, walls, and steps are all beyond its pay grade.
entries.content:
The market is stuffed to the gills with pool-scrubbing robots that cost thousands of dollars, and consumers are well justified in worrying whether that level of expense will ultimately be worthwhile. But there’s also a subset of pool robots that go the other way—much simpler devices that cost well under $500, sometimes much less.

It’s here where we find the Poolease X1, a pint-sized robot that can be yours for barely over 100 bucks. Can it possibly be any good?

Mini and on the Move

I’ve tested robots along these lines in the past. All work under the same general principle. Stripped down to the basics, the tiny Poolease X1—just 9 pounds in weight and not much larger than a lunch box—has no spinning brushes or treads to propel it. Rather, the clearly Dyson-inspired robot is entirely powered by water jets, which send it on a largely random zigzag path around the pool while pulling debris up through the bottom of the device.

Because of this simple propulsion system, the X1 can’t clean walls or the waterline or even steps, nor can it “scrub” the way a robot with motorized rollers can. It’s strictly limited to the floor of the pool. Needless to say there are no wireless or mobile app features at this price level, either.

There’s also no debris basket on the X1, per se. Rather, the entire device splits into two, and leaves and other debris are simply captured inside it, with a simple filter screen serving to keep debris from passing through the device and back out though the propulsion system’s exhaust port. To clean the device, you snap open four clips surrounding the chassis to separate the halves, then spray the whole thing down with a hose.

entries.title: Bumble Tried to Change Dating, but the Dating Market Forced It to Change Instead
entries.summary: The app now allows men to make the first move, suggesting its women-first positioning was limiting growth. It joins other dating apps now throwing everything at the wall in a bid to stay relevant.
entries.content:
Not even 24 hours after dating app Bumble announced it was getting rid of its trademark feature that requires women to make the first move, Robin H.’s inbox was already attracting unwanted attention.

“This guy responded to my prompt, and he wasn’t a person I would have swiped on. I can’t believe some of these men think we’re a match,” the 53-year-old social worker in Orlando, Florida, tells WIRED. “Men will swipe on anybody and see what sticks. And with this change, they are just going to be reaching out to everybody.” (Citing privacy concerns, Robin asked that WIRED not publish her full last name.)

Bumble, which hit the market in December 2014, staked its brand on challenging traditional heterosexual dating dynamics. “Whitney Wolfe Is Bringing Feminism to Your Phone,” an Austin Woman headline exclaimed less than two years after launch. But the app’s sudden reversal last week suggests its women-first positioning has become a liability to the company’s sustainability.

Bumble’s policy update—which includes giving matches 72 hours to respond; previously it was 24—comes as Big Dating’s growth is lagging. Perhaps hinting at what was to come, in May, Bumble CEO Whitney Wolfe-Herd said in an interview with Axios that niche apps aren’t built for real longevity. The dilemma is emblematic of the volatility in the current dating market, where declining engagement and the introduction of AI are forcing companies to rethink how they should best appeal to singles.

These problems aren’t unique to Bumble. Match Group’s August 2026 results showed Tinder’s number of daily active users is down 4 percent from the previous year, while Hinge’s global monthly active users rose 13 percent during the same period. But even apps with sustained engagement struggle with brand perception issues.

Feeld, a niche kink app that championed polyamory and BDSM in its early days, has shifted its focus to attracting more vanilla users, resulting in a 200 percent spike in users in 2025, though people have described the new vibe as “normie hell.”

Likewise, Grindr has positioned itself as more than an app for hookups, expanding into a “gayborhood” that offers luxury travel experiences, medical prescriptions for GLP-1s and erectile dysfunction pills, musical artist activations, and AI matchmaking. To turn a profit, Grindr has essentially transformed into a digital gated community that now charges members $500 to hook up through its newest membership tier, Edge, while users who opt out are forced to navigate a platform drowning in ads and bots.

Bumble, which is privately owned and reportedly exploring a sale, has taken a similar route: transforming a once-niche product into a for-everybody service that pay-gates basic features. The move has not settled well with users online, who have renamed it “Yellow Tinder”—a reference to the color of its logo—and complained that the changes will encourage harassment. “I’m not going to use an app that makes me feel like prey,” one user wrote on X.

“The change obviously goes against their whole thing,” says Emily Spence, a 28-year-old events producer in New York City who has used Bumble since 2015. “But the requirement for women to message first didn’t really prevent creeps from messaging you. Just because you say ‘hey’ first doesn’t mean a man isn’t gonna send you something crazy after. It was kind of like a false sense of protection.”

The new update may also reflect a desire for a return to more traditional courtship roles. In the announcement, the company noted that 66 percent of women surveyed on Bumble said they prefer men to send the first message, adding that it alleviates unnecessary pressure from the experience.

The company said that its testing of the new feature showed increased chat initiation, but it’s unclear if that will actually translate to more dates and higher user retention or just more unwanted messages. Bumble did not respond to a request for comment.

Stefanie Feldman, 41, appreciates the new direction of the app. “I like that it takes off the pressure. Sometimes I just want the men to do the work,” says the business manager in Los Angeles. “I’ve never considered myself a feminist. I want to be pursued. And just because someone reaches out to you doesn’t mean you have to say anything. So that is a feminine power in itself, learning to say no.”

Even before last week’s news, Bumble’s brand dilution seems to have been in the works for a while. In 2024, Bumble began tweaking its founding principle when it debuted the feature Opening Moves, which let men reply to a prompt on a user’s page. According to data the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with WIRED, the app has also not featured its women-first social mission as part of its marketing in the US since 2023, with only a few limited branding spots reinforcing that women make the first move in 2022. As an alternative, Bumble “created more generic messaging on how the app has been successful for previous users and encouraged potential users to ‘get to know new people today,’” says Kara Lee, a senior analyst with the firm.

The reversal ultimately highlights the difficulty of building a dating app around a social mission and how the cost of doing business sometimes requires you to abandon your original ideals.

Riki Thompson, an associate professor of digital rhetoric at the University of Washington Tacoma who published a study on the app last year, adds that the shift away from mandatory first moves was the only way, in the interim, for Bumble to keep pace with its rivals.

“An app is only one small part of a much larger system, how people actually behave, what they expect from dating, and the norms they bring with them. You can design an app with great intentions, but you can’t fully control how people use it,” Thompson says in an email. “Bumble is still a business. It has to stay competitive and profitable in a marketplace where plenty of competitors aren’t built around any social mission at all.”

entries.title: The 3 Best USB Phone Chargers (2026): Anker, DeWalt
entries.summary: I put top-rated USB car chargers to the test for fast charging, value, heat, and safety. These are the best I found.
entries.content:
A car charger is not a complicated device. The best USB car charger is the one that charges your phone quickly, does not overheat, allows multiple devices to charge, and remains compatible with whichever USB cable you (or your passengers) happen to have available. It is usually also a trusted brand, with certification to international standards—not a janky gas station charger that'll blow a fuse with an internal short or offer insufficient protection against dust and debris.

I put car chargers to the test with ammeters and phone apps, and on multi-hour road trips, to make sure each one lived up to its promises. The best car charger I've found is the three-port Anker 167.5W Nano ($38), which combines 100-watt fast-charging capability for auxiliary devices, plus dual-port USB-Cs, USB-A capability, and safety features that include overheat protection.

If you shun dangling cords, I offer the Anker 75W Fast Charger ($30) with slightly lower top amperage but a retractable cable. And for families whose kids can't live without constant tablets in the back seat, there's the DeWalt 72W Front and Back Seat Charger ($45).

For other power needs, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Portable Jump Starters, Best Power Banks, Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations.

The Best USB Car Charger

This three-port charger from Anker offers pretty much everything I want from a USB car charger while remaining hearteningly compact and affordable. The 100W fast-charging USB-C port kicks out nearly 7 amps at top speeds, enough juice to charge my Macbook Air to 50 percent in about 25 minutes, before fast-charging slows down, and does the same for my iPhone. But especially, Anker's PowerIQ technology smartly assesses the differing voltage needs of various phones to avoid over- or under-voltage. I've never actually seen this Anker on sale on Amazon above $40.

It also doesn't hurt that Anker makes some of WIRED's most trusted portable power technology—tech whose reliability we've verified over years of real-world testing. You don't overwhelmingly want a janky cheap charger that blows a fuse. Good insulation and a tiny built-in fan effectively lower overheating versus other fast-chargers, though you'll still notice some heat when charging at 100 watts or above. USB-A capability is welcome for versatility, though my testing showed somewhat lower power than advertised on that port.

Either way, I was able to charge both my top-pick portable jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox ($120), in a little over an hour while also keeping my phone topped off on a road trip—which is pretty much as high-demand as I get while also blasting AC and the radio, and this caused no problems with the 15-amp circuit on my older car. But note that while most modern cars run on 20-amp fuses, the max capacity for this charger when drawing from all three ports does run pretty close to the max load for an older-model car charger. The charger is able to draw quite close to the maximum amperage on a 15-amp fuse.

A similar budget pick: The lower overheating on my top-pick Anker bodes well for longevity, which means it might still be a cheaper option in the long haul. But note that a similar three-port fast-charger from Chinese brand Ugreen ($21) performed comparably on charging speeds. But it also got significantly hotter within 10 minutes of fast-charging.

Best USB Car Charger With Retractable Cord

A retractable charging cable has the distinct merit of keeping your car tidy, without dangling charging cords to get tangled between your foot and the gas pedal. It also obviates the need to remember a cable at all. This Anker model offers a 2-foot cable that retracts quite easily back into its base after a quick tug on the cable, neat as you'd like. The cable's 45W fast-charging capability will max out the charging capability of most iPhones.

Anker is a brand I trust for charging technology. But it's worth noting that retractable cables introduce a couple failure points that could lower longevity. The cable can't be swapped out if it gets worn, and the retraction mechanism itself could wear out. Tidiness has a price, it seems. This said, the charger is not overly expensive, usually retailing closer to $20.

Best Front and Back Seat Car Charger

The modern car family involves a nest of devices—parents in the front seat charging phones, children in the back with tablets, somehow watching the same thing over and over. And nothing ends the peace of a road trip quite like a tablet running out of juice halfway through an episode of Bluey.

This DeWalt is a good solution, offering decent (but not great) 30-watt charging on the USB-C port for front-seat parents, and a couple of auxiliary USB-A ports to keep maintenance charge on backseat devices. DeWalt is a power tool brand, of course, and so these ports were likely designed for a tool or two resting in the back seat. But kids have tools, too, and this'll serve their needs.

It's perhaps frustrating that the back seat chargers are USB-A. But I haven't found a good USB charger with a back-seat USB-C charging setup, assuming your car doesn't have a back seat charger of its own. And so while this DeWalt is a compromise, it's the best compromise I've found so far.

Frequently Asked Questions

How I Selected and Tested USB Car Chargers

For this round of car-charger testing, I looked first for known quantities and trusted charging technology brands like Anker, Belkin, and Ugreen. I also ordered and tested devices that other credible sources had ranked as their favorite USB chargers, making sure that each charger is broadly available and easy to find. Needless to say, I only assessed and recommend UL-certified chargers, and avoided dodgy-looking brands: Short circuits in cars aren't fun, for me or for you.

I then set about testing the claims for each car charger, using ammeters for each port on each charger, testing with an ammeter while pulling max loads. I additionally used the Ampere phone app to test the peak draw for a Motorola Razr and an iPhone 13, and also tested to see whether the charger heated up while pulling max draw—both using the phone app and an infrared thermometer.

I tested with each charger's included cord, where relevant, but also with a fast-charging cable on USB-C devices that advertise this capability. For my top contenders among 100-watt fast chargers, I also tested to see how long it took to charge a Macbook Air M4 and my top-pick jump starter, the 4000A Wolfbox.

As with every device tested by the WIRED Reviews team, I subjected my top-pick chargers to real-world road tests. I went on multi-hour road trips with devices plugged in. I charged portable jump starters or laptops while also charging phones. I tested durability in real-world conditions that may also involve grubby fingers. I assessed each device not just for brute speed, but for versatility in different use cases. For now, I favor chargers that offer both USB-C and USB-A capability, so as not to leave any devices out in the cold.

I also checked up on customer reviews for each of these chargers. If I saw any customer complaints, I tried my darndest to replicate them. I jammed chargers in and out of the ports, and wobbled the chargers around in their sockets. I acted the way people act when they're fumbling for a device charger they're not looking at while driving.

Are Cheap USB Chargers Unsafe?

I've put a bit of emphasis on trusted brands while testing USB chargers, and this isn't by accident. The world is full of dodgy gas station or Amazon chargers, and bad cables, with insufficient electrical insulation and inconsistent current delivery.

Bad USB-C cables and electrical insulation are known fire hazards in the worst cases, but inconsistent voltage is also just bad for your phone or laptop battery over time. Poorly made chargers, connectors, and cables can have higher resistance (leading to overheating), bad or inconsistent connections, and poor protections against shorts and surges. All of these things are bad. At worst, they can fry your device or lower your battery longevity.

As a rule of thumb, look for language that a product is “UL-Listed” or "UL-Certified" not merely "UL-Classified" or “Recognized.” The latter two mean that a product has been tested only against specific hazards or under specific conditions. Listed and Certified products have fully passed all tests within a given standard. WIRED will only recommend chargers that are UL-listed or -certified.

Other USB Chargers I Recommend

Scosche PowerVolt 60W Dual-Port Charger for $20: This dual-port USB-C charger from California car brand Scosche is the simplest thing imaginable. Two USB-C ports, each separately rated at 30 watts. Each charges quickly and is reliable. Though this Scosche doesn't offer a fast-charging option for laptops, it's perfectly optimized for a pair of phones—and admirably low-cost. If you're mostly just going to charge a phone, this is a tight runner-up to my top-pick Anker—especially if you're pretty sure you'll never need a USB-A charger in your car.

Anker 40W Two-Port Charger for $20: Like the Scosche, this Anker is a purpose-driven phone charger with two USB-C ports. It's a little lower-powered than the Scosche, with a little less juice than the newest generation of phones can support. But the price is right if you're willing to accept lower charging speeds.

Belkin BoostCharge 42W Dual-Port Charger for $24: This compact, well-insulated dual-port charger from California tech accessory brand Belkin is great as a budget option, with decently fast USB-C and USB-A charging. Just note that the tiny device might be a bit shallow for some deeper car chargers, and that when plugged in, the charger has a nonnegotiable and oddly bright LED light that stays on even when no device is charging. This won't bother you unless it bothers you.

Nekteck 45W Two-Port Car Charger for $32: This basic, bare-bones Neckteck charger is a decent compromise for those who need fast charging on a QC 3.0-compatible USB-A device. While a 45-watt max speed for USB-C charging isn't fast by modern standards, it's still faster than most phones. And the QC 3.0 USB-A charger is significantly faster than most USB-A chargers, for those with older devices.

Lisen 90W Charger With Cord for $20: This charger from Chinese car-tech company Lisen performed reasonably well in testing, though true fast-charging isn't available and the listed charge speeds are a little confusing and don't add up. The coiled cord is not able to be retracted or removed, making this charger a bit ungainly for daily use, but the option on a 60- or 90-inch cord does make this Lisen the rare device suitable for charging a USB-C phone or tablet in the back seat. This said, I tested a shorter cable, and longer USB-C cables are notoriously finicky for high amperage.

Also Tested

The six-port Ai Aikenuo back seat charging kit is useful for keeping a large number of devices charged up for work use or larger families, but it disappeared from Amazon right before this guide's publication. I'll monitor to see if this is a momentary glitch or whether it's been discontinued.

entries.title: A MAGA County’s Top Election Official Wants to Hire Election Denial Superstar Tina Peters
entries.summary: Tina Peters was convicted of seven counts related to election interference in 2024. Now, she’s fielding an offer from a county that’s become a hotbed of voting-related conspiracy theories.
entries.content:
Last week, Clint Curtis, the top election official in Shasta County, California, publicly accused members of his own staff of bypassing security, which he later claimed was an attempt “to sabotage a federal election.”

Days later, Curtis announced plans to hire a new deputy: Tina Peters, the election denial superstar who was convicted of seven counts related to election interference in 2024 and sentenced to nine years in prison.

Peters, the former clerk of Mesa County, Colorado, has yet to publicly comment on the offer, but her lawyer Peter Ticktin tells WIRED she “is giving consideration to helping in the efforts in Shasta County, as there most definitely has been monkey business in the way the election was handled.”

Peters was convicted after she allowed Conan Hayes, a former pro surfer who later worked for pillow salesman turned election denier Mike Lindell, unauthorized access to election equipment in Mesa County as part of a scheme to prove that the 2020 presidential election had been stolen from Donald Trump. (Hayes was never charged for his role in the scheme). Colorado governor Jared Polis commuted Peters’ sentence in May after months of pressure from President Trump, who purported to have issued his own pardon even though Peters was convicted on state charges. Recently released court papers show how Trump and his advisers coordinated with federal agencies to cut federal funding and grants to Colorado as part of a pressure campaign to free Peters.

Curtis told The Guardian that Peters would not have access to the county’s voting system but refused to specify what her duties would include. Curtis did not respond to a request for comment.

Should Peters accept the role, she would likely feel right at home in Shasta County, a deep-red enclave in Northern California that has become ground zero for many of the election denial conspiracy theories promoted by Trump and his supporters over the past six years. And in Curtis, she would be working alongside a man who has a decades-long history of promoting many of the same election-related conspiracy theories she herself has championed.

“This should be stopped immediately: Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis is trying to hire election-denier Tina Peters to collude with the Trump administration’s election mischief,” US senator Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, wrote on Facebook.

Curtis first came to national prominence more than two decades ago, when he claimed to have created a software program that could rig elections without election officials being able to notice anything amiss. Curtis, who testified before Congress about his program, said he did this at the behest of Florida state lawmaker Tom Feeney, who denied the claim.

In 2025, when the previous Registrar of Voters in Shasta County, Thomas Toller. retired midterm, Curtis put his name forward for the position, despite having no experience in running elections and spending most of his career working as a lawyer and a computer developer. He also lived in Florida at the time and had no ties to the area.

During the 2025 interview process for his current role, Curtis touted his associations with prominent figures in the election denial community, including Lindell, disgraced former national security adviser Mike Flynn, and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon.

Since his appointment, Curtis has faced a string of accusations about his behavior from members of his staff. An internal investigation concluded that he had physically threatened, verbally abused, and retaliated against staff at the Shasta County Elections Office, while an external investigation found he had retaliated against them. Among the specific allegations made by his colleagues were that Curtis threatened to have one employee dragged out by her hair and to “throat-punch” another. Curtis has consistently denied the allegations.

In June, Curtis lost his bid to keep his job past this year when Joanna Francescut, who worked in elections in Shasta County for 18 years, easily defeated him. Curtis had fired Francescut days after he took up his role.

The Board of Supervisors in Shasta County, having initially voted against censuring Curtis, last week voted 3-1 to censure him. However, Curtis responded to the public rebuke by making further allegations against his staff, including claims that they were bypassing security to tamper with elections. He subsequently invited the media back to his office to show them CCTV footage of one staff member opening a door without using a keycard.

When asked if he had asked the employee in question what he was doing, Curtis said he hadn’t.

"Shasta County has gone through a lot of controversy, division, and animosity related to elections, and based on the initial response from the public I’ve received already, recruiting Tina Peters would increase this and reduce trust in our elections," Matt Plummer, a member of the Shasta Board of Supervisors, tells WIRED, while acknowledging Curtis has the authority to make his own hiring decisions. The other members did not respond to a request for comment.

Plummer isn’t the only authority raising questions about the proposal. Stewart Buettell, the deputy CEO of the County of Shasta, tells WIRED, “There has been no formal process or application submitted to replace the current assistant registrar of voters,” adding that “any prospective employee would go through the same hiring process as anyone else seeking employment with the county.”

Brent Turner, the current assistant registrar of voters, told Shasta Scout on Tuesday that he was surprised to hear he may be replaced. “I believe I’m the assistant registrar. And if anything changes I will certainly let you know,” said Turner.

Curtis told the Redding Record Searchlight that he would be hiring Peters as a consultant as a way of circumventing what he predicted would be the county’s efforts to block the appointment. He said that as a consultant, she would be able to continue to work in Colorado and Washington, DC while also at times supervising onsite in Shasta County.

Buettell said that if Peters was hired as a consultant that would “typically require a contract for services, consistent with Shasta County policy, which has not been initiated.”

While there has been strong criticism of the effort to employ Peters, some election experts believe mechanisms are in place to prevent it from actually happening.

"This announcement seems to be nothing more than performance art by the current and outgoing clerk, who was rejected by voters in the primary,” David Becker, the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research and a former Justice Department lawyer, tells WIRED. “It’s highly questionable that county officials could spend any taxpayer dollars on this or give any authority to a convicted and unrepentant felon like Ms. Peters.”

Despite her parole conditions barring her from travelling outside Colorado without permission, Peters has spent the months since her release appearing in-person at multiple MAGA events as well as numerous interviews with right-wing podcasters, continuing to promote election denial conspiracy theories. She has also met with Trump in the Oval Office and has claimed to have met the head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and presented her plan to secure elections.

If Peters does decide to take up the role in Shasta County, which Curtis told Action News Now would begin on September 4, it will allow her time to fulfil one more public engagement, when she is scheduled to speak at the Destroying the Whore of Babylon conference later this month.

entries.title: How Teen ‘After-Prom’ Kings in LA Monetized the High School Rager
entries.summary: The West Coast house-party scene has long been iconic. For these young, tech-savvy entrepreneurs, it was also inspiration for MyPlots, a party-promotion empire.
entries.content:
When I ask Jack Schwartz how much he’s charging for a table at his upcoming party in Manhattan, he offers to “show” me instead of answering with words. Then, the 21-year-old reaches into his black leather jacket, pulls out a white envelope containing $27,500 in cash—neatly separated into three stacks—and slides it across a countertop at WIRED’s office in New York, his right hand flashing a $10,000 diamond- and sapphire-encrusted gold ring.

Schwartz is the founder and CEO of MyPlots, a party promotion and ticketing company he started after throwing a series of legendary ragers in Los Angeles beginning at the precocious age of 14. He’s been building a cult of personality since high school, teasing his parties on Instagram and Snap to create FOMO and then packaging highlights in Reels and Stories afterward. “He was like The Great Gatsby,” says Zane Harwin, a 19-year-old former high school classmate of Schwartz’s who now does marketing for MyPlots. “That’s what we would all call him.” Harwin has traveled to New York with Schwartz for the party, and to try to raise money for their app. He’s wearing a $500 white Chrome Hearts T-shirt, a 424 jacket, and a claspless silver “permanent” bracelet he got at Coachella.

MyPlots launched its namesake app in January 2025, in part to promote “after-prom” events for high schoolers. Today, it’s the go-to app for under-21s in LA and boasts more than 1 million users. The app is also expanding its user base to older (of-age) attendees. Daniel Herring, a 30-year-old promoter who works with MyPlots, says that when he moved to LA three years ago, most events were promoted on Partiful, but “over the last year, it’s definitely been damn near all MyPlots.”

On MyPlots, a host will sign up, create an event, and invite people. The app allows promoters to target people who have attended their parties in the past and text guests updates, but it does not share phone numbers with promoters or third parties for off-platform use. Guests RSVP and purchase their tickets through the app, and the company takes a 20 percent cut of all sales. (When it launched last year, the ticketing feature distinguished MyPlots from competitors, but they’re catching up. In June, Partiful announced it would be offering in-app ticketing.) To use MyPlots, users technically need to be 18, but Schwartz concedes that “people find ways around that.” Stripe, which is integrated into the app, allows users as young as 13 if they have a parent enrolled on the account.

It’s not really the tech that sets MyPlots apart, which feels amateur compared to competitors like Partiful. Rather, it's the cool young crowd using it for exclusive, luxury parties—and how MyPlots markets to them. Scanning the app in mid July 2026 turned up an all-ages rap show at downtown LA nightclub The Mayan; a mansion party in Encino boasting “CELEBERTIES [sic]”—with a disclaimer that organizers aren’t liable for “anything negative that could happen” before, during, and after the event; and an 18-plus Daybreak Festival at the W Hollywood hotel featuring “VIP cabanas” and Schwartz’s bolded name as a headlining DJ. Ticket pricing is often tiered, sometimes varying based on gender, timing, or VIP access. A “Euphoria Mansion Party” from last spring, which did not specify an age restriction, boasted 500-plus expected guests and offered 30 minutes of “bedroom access” for $75.

No longer just a rite of passage or a chance to score clout at school, teen parties are now full-blown moneymaking enterprises for entrepreneurs savvy enough to take advantage. In addition to MyPlots, there are promoters like 310 Events, Off Campus Events, and LA Social, and ticketing apps like Plots and Turnt, all catering to young crowds.

“If you get real creative, there's always a way to make money—even without even leaving your house—if you know how to market and you can use the internet,” says Schwartz, whose role model is billionaire Mark Cuban. “So many young people are just on their phones all day.”

Standing at 5'8", Schwartz wears his dirty blond hair slicked back, and often has a pair of Oakleys perched on top of his head. He speaks with the bullish confidence of a tech founder, the occasional "like" reminding you of his age. As he tells it, he first became an entrepreneur at 14 years old. While a freshman at Palisades Charter High School—a well-known public school known as “Pali” by locals—he started a streetwear line called Loonar Clothing. His marketing strategy was to wait outside of celebrity haunts like Boa Steakhouse and the Saddle Ranch Chop House “for like 8 to 12 hours” and ask stars like Addison Rae to wear his T-shirts, sunglasses, and other swag on camera—prompting an Inside Edition story. Just before the Covid-19 pandemic hit, Schwartz threw three parties in succession, building a name for himself at school. “Everyone was like, who is this Jack Schwartz kid?” he recalls. “Every kid at Pali, even the seniors, are going.”

The first was in a rec room at his dad’s apartment complex, with his dad working security and collecting payments; the other two were on Hollywood Boulevard, where he paid $2,000 cash to rent the space. Schwartz says it wasn’t hard to find venues willing to rent to minors. “If you go to Hollywood, some of these venues … they'll do anything for business.”

His parties weren’t always hosted at official venues; they popped up at warehouses, offices, even friends’ houses. “A lot of the time, the parents … wouldn't care,” Schwartz says. “They would be upstairs, and it would be in their backyard.” But this wasn’t always drama-free: One of his New Year’s Eve parties, held at a warehouse, got shut down prematurely because the cops showed up and Schwartz claims the venue didn’t have the right permit.

Schwartz isn’t the only promoter who says it’s relatively easy for underage kids to find a party venue in LA—if they have money. Matt, a venue operator in his twenties who caters to brands and celebrities, started a party-promoting Instagram account as a teen and recalls renting corporate space and buying insurance for the night on sites like Eventhelper.com or Eventsured for a couple hundred bucks. (Neither website returned a request for comment.) Asked how he secured insurance as a minor, he says he “probably” put it under his dad’s name or figured out another way of getting around it. (WIRED has given Matt a pseudonym as he’d like to avoid professional repercussions.) “Some people are desperate for money,” he offers, by way of explaining why adults would work with children and take on the liability that comes with it.

And the liabilities are many. Matt recalls that a dance studio in Brentwood, which he rented for an event while in high school, hosted another party with teen guests months later. The floor broke under the weight of the crowd. Los Angeles Magazine reported that it sent “rowdy rich kids spilling into the streets.” As a venue operator, Matt says he’s worked with “really kind, sweet high schoolers” and teen promoters who cut corners. Some hire their friends as security guards or sneak alcohol in via staging equipment. The underage guests themselves present additional problems, sometimes showing up visibly drunk and getting aggressive when they’re not allowed in.

In 2024, Schwartz appeared in Social Studies, an FX documentary series about the highs and lows of teen social media use. According to the doc, in 2022, Schwartz hosted his own birthday party, in concert with another friend. In a social media post about the event, guests were explicitly advised against bringing “visible alcohol.” Nonetheless, the show depicted the party’s debaucherous turn: drinking out of containers, smoking, hooking up, a fight among two girls, and a teenage boy hanging off an indoor balcony railing. Guests interviewed say someone threw up before passing out on the ground. His friends called an ambulance, but not before dragging him a few blocks to avoid getting the party planners in trouble. “That’s scary,” Schwartz tells the camera in a follow-up interview. “That’s also why we purchased insurance.” When asked about the FX series, Schwartz tells me he was misrepresented by the filmmakers. He now claims the birthday party in question wasn’t his, that he didn’t organize or manage it, and as such, he didn’t get insurance. FX declined to comment.

In Schwartz’s junior year, when Covid-19 lockdowns lifted, teens were desperate for in-person connection; he decided to go hard, throwing parties under the brand MyPlots—“plot” is slang for something to do—and advertised them on Instagram. But it was “messy,” he says, with people sending him money via Venmo and Zelle or paying cover charges (typically $20) at the door. Sometimes security guards would pocket the money. “There had to be a better way to facilitate these events, make them safer, and provide people with more security,” he recalls. “So that's why I created MyPlots.”

To bolster his business, Schwartz grew his TikTok following to 1.6 million by doing man-on-the-street videos asking people how much their fits cost; he also inked a deal with Snap’s Spotlight monetization program for a “lot” of money, picking up a “ton of followers,” he says. (Snap did not respond to requests for comment.) In 2023, during his senior year, Schwartz used proceeds from his parties to buy a blue BMW M340i that he says cost $50,000.

Zane Harwin was a freshman at Pali when Schwartz was a junior. The former captain of the school’s surf team, Harwin is 6'4”, with a mischievous smile and has brown hair that flows in beachy waves. He towers over his boss, but has always looked up to Schwartz. Harwin fondly recalls rolling up to one of Schwartz’s giant house parties in Brentwood, seeing cars lined down the road and Schwartz dutifully running the door. “He’s the man of the party,” Harwin says, adding that his proximity to the enterprise means some girls have offered to do “anything” to get into the events. (He says he would never take them up on that.) As a duo, they’re a modern-day Spencer Pratt and Brody Jenner—Schwartz is the brains of the operation, and Harwin the charm.

They speak with nostalgia about the chaos of their high school raging—parties in iconic LA neighborhoods like Beverly Hills and Bel Air—some so crowded that people would fall into the hot tub. Another Pali classmate and now MyPlots’ head of marketing, Lucas Ward, remembers seeing a kid “literally get knocked out cold” during a fight. “Kids would make it a mess, but it was authentic high school parties,” Harwin says.

MyPlots likely could not have been born anywhere but the affluent neighborhoods of West LA, where many teens have easy access to cars, envy-inducing houses, wealth, and the jaw-dropping beauty of the Pacific Ocean’s coastline. Zillow pegs the average home price in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood at just over $3 million. Pali High is so iconic that there was once a popular TikTok account devoted to sharing the outfits of its students. As is typical for kids in this area, both Schwartz and Harwin grew up well-off. Schwartz's mother runs a marketing agency while his father has a corporate job; Harwin is the child of a tv personality/producer and a restaurateur/hospitality real estate developer.

“It's like the number one place if you want to be an influencer,” says Harwin. “Social media is the biggest here. Hollywood, everyone knows a person in LA, and like you post one video here, it'll go viral.”

Rachel, a Culver City–based mother of a 17-year-old son and 15-year-old daughter, says both of her kids and their friends attend ticketed parties thrown by other teens, which are promoted on social media; her son’s friend has a “business” throwing parties at other people’s homes. Teenagers in the LA area “can stay out really late and, you know, just take a Waymo and be very independent,” she says. The fact that “everyone has their parents’ credit card on their phone” is a game changer, she adds. “Kids are just kind of absent-mindedly spending a lot of money.”

Outside of lavish locations, these teen parties are markedly different from the ones you hosted in the backyard when your parents went out of town. Rachel’s daughter, Amber, says parties are typically advertised on Instagram and Snapchat, and the location is dropped the day of the event. Usually, girls’ tickets cost less than guys’, and kids can prepay, showing a barcode at the door. The hosts, some of them teens themselves, use an app to sell tickets. Most crucially, they’re making real money off parties that 20 years ago would have just gotten you grounded.

In May 2025—just a few months after the launch of MyPlots—Schwartz and Harwin threw an “after-prom tour,” hosting parties for seniors to attend once their school proms ended. Harwin advertised the party “tours” on Instagram, filming from exotic cars and penthouses with stunning mountain views, sometimes using stacks of cash as props. “Nobody else in the world has done a tour like this,” he said in one reel, sitting on stone steps behind a swimming pool. Their strategy for selling tickets was getting popular high school seniors to act as brand ambassadors—a role that Harwin filled when he was still a student at Pali.

As is common with after-prom ragers, things sometimes got out of hand. Several attendees of one party say security for the event got aggressive and shoved students. Schwartz brushes this aside, first claiming that the security came with the venue and later that too many students tried to get their friends in for free. “It was like a shit show,” he says. “The crowd was so disrespectful.”

Raine, a 16-year-old who lives in Venice, attended a backyard party in the Rancho Park neighborhood advertised on MyPlots and Instagram last March. (Rachel, Amber, and Raine are all pseudonyms, in order to protect their privacy.) As they were leaving, at around 10 pm, Raine saw a girl, clearly intoxicated, lying on the grass in the front yard. The fire department showed up. The account promoting the party later posted an Instagram story with the text: “two drunk ho** ruined the party for yall NEXT ONE GON BE CRAZY.”

Schwartz wants to distance himself from promoters who use his app. He says the technology is simply facilitating ticket sales and that he has no connection to the majority of the parties on MyPlots—nor does he bear any legal responsibility. “I have no idea who 95 percent of [the promoters] are,” he says, adding that he’s very selective about what events he personally throws. “It's not worth the liability to make a few thousand dollars.”

Marley Majcher, who plans events in LA through her business The Party Goddess!, is skeptical that young party promoters are free from liability, even when they have single-night insurance. Majcher organizes high-end events, including sweet sixteens and bar and bat mitzvahs in locations like Beverly Hills and Malibu. She says her own lawyer has stressed the importance of airtight contracts to account for things like accidents and drinking and driving. “There's just no way that these people have the coverage for what they need to have … especially here, where we're very sue-happy and affluent,” says Majcher, who is 56 but tells me that she looks younger “due to the amount of Botox and skin treatments I have on a regular basis.”

William Lemmon, the principal broker at Broadway Insurance Services, says that a party host would generally need a special event permit, an occupancy sign-off if the space isn't zoned for a crowd—like a warehouse or office—the fire marshal's approval, and a permit for alcohol sales, which a minor can't apply for. Instant online insurance is perfectly fine when everyone's an adult, but if “a teenager is charging a cover at a warehouse with booze, that's about as far from the intended use as it can get,” he says. He also points out that minors generally can't be held to contracts, so the carrier could argue the policy is invalid. Liability for these events is a “pile-on” that would involve the promoter, tenant, property owner, whoever bought alcohol, and possibly parents if the party thrower is underage. “Here’s what it really comes down to: Take that same party and make everyone 21, and it’s insurable. Add minors and alcohol, and no carrier will knowingly touch it.”

For now, the business is working. Following the successful 2025 after-prom tour, Schwartz and Harwin say they took a monthslong European vacation, flying first class and hitting Amsterdam and Ibiza, among other spots. Despite Ibiza’s reputation as one of the party capitals of the world—with clubs open all night and after-hours gatherings that last the entire next day—the guys decided to throw their own event at their villa.

“We go to this post office, we create a flyer, and we're printing out like hundreds of flyers,” Harwin recalls, detailing how they went to the massive outdoor club Ushuaïa and threw the posters into the crowd. “The next thing we know, we go back to the villa, and there's already a line.” They claim they charged $100 a head and walked away with around $10,000. When I ask why they felt the need to work during a vacation, Harwin says they missed the hustle: “This is what we do. We’re good at this.”

By early June 2026, Schwartz had transitioned to throwing parties for an 18-plus crowd—and taken his talents to the East Coast. A few hours after the meeting at WIRED’s office, I head to HK Hall, a two-story nightclub in Manhattan’s Hell’s Kitchen neighborhood. Schwartz and the MyPlots team are hosting an after-party for Houston rapper Don Toliver’s Madison Square Garden show—the one with a $27,500 table fee. It’s their second big New York City event, the first being a Playboi Carti after-party last November.

By 10:30 pm, a couple dozen young-looking people are in line at the door, which is being manned by Ward and Schwartz. A woman tries to haggle with Schwartz to get a discount on the $100 entry fee. He offers it to her for $75, but when she gets to Ward, he still charges her $100, telling her the extra is “tax.”

A white guy in a Bathing Ape shirt, with beaded box braids, is smoking a joint outside. It’s Daniel Herring, the aforementioned event promoter. Schwartz and his collaborators flew him out from LA. He’s a few feet away from a sign prohibiting drugs but says that, because he’s a VIP, security is holding on to his half-ounce of weed. “I chose MyPlots over a lot of these guys,” says Herring, who promotes his parties on MyPlots because he favors its customer service. “They’re very driven, they’re very humble, and they’re genuine. They’re not out here sharking or doing bad business by anybody.”

Inside the club are bottle girls with sparklers, people smoking hookah, and at least a couple of influencers livestreaming. Eight TVs repeatedly flash MyPlots’ purple logo. The place fills up quickly; By midnight, hundreds of people are lined up around the block. Schwartz says he paid “a substantial amount of money” for Toliver’s 2 am appearance.

MyPlots is in the middle of a search for angel investors, hoping to raise $10 million to set up a permanent office and hire a sales team to book talent for parties. It’s also planning a 10,000-person festival on Santa Monica beach for next summer. Schwartz is currently taking a hiatus from pursuing his economics degree at UCLA, explaining, “Every kid you know, from back in the day, they wanted to be a policeman, a firefighter. Now everyone wants to be a YouTuber, a streamer.” His ambitions go far beyond nightlife. He says he wants to eventually sell the company and start a new business: “Something in AI.”

Harwin puts the long-term goal more plainly: “Make as much money as I possibly can—as soon as I can.”

“It’s very possible,” Harwin says, “we're going to be doing something bigger than Coachella once we get older.” You know, once they’re 25.

entries.title: Salmonella Is Everywhere
entries.summary: From granola to guacamole, a wide variety of foods have been recalled lately over salmonella risks. Experts say common-sense precautions go a long way.
entries.content:
Just as the US’s explosive diarrhea situation is starting to improve, there seem to be fresh new food risks to worry about. Jalapeño peppers, eggs, granola, and even dog food are being recalled because of possible contamination with salmonella bacteria.

A growing outbreak related to contaminated jalapeños is responsible for 431 illnesses in 32 states, with 57 people requiring hospitalization, according to an August 19 update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The agency has identified jalapeños from Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors as the source of the outbreak. The company agreed to recall affected produce, triggering widespread removals of salsa, guacamole, salad dressing, and other jalapeño-containing products across Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods, Kroger, Target, and other stores. Chipotle and Qdoba also stopped serving the jalapeños in question.

A separate salmonella outbreak linked to eggs has sickened 98 people across 17 states. Of those, 26 have been hospitalized. Health officials have named Midwest Poultry Services as a common egg source but say the company’s eggs did not account for all illnesses in the outbreak and are investigating other sources. The company in July began a voluntary recall of 19 million eggs due to potential contamination. The eggs were produced and distributed from farms in Texas.

A type of granola—Lacnola Lactation Granola from Hampton Grocers—is also being recalled due to possible salmonella risk. In that case, the problematic ingredient is organic moringa powder, a nutrient-dense green powder made from the leaves of the South Asian moringa tree. Several salmonella outbreaks linked to imported moringa leaf powder and dietary supplements containing moringa have occurred since last year.

Salmonella is also making its way into dog food. Oma’s Pride is recalling bags of its Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe after the FDA received a consumer complaint and subsequently collected and analyzed a sample of the product, which tested positive for salmonella. Three illnesses in dogs have been reported, according to the FDA notice.

Salmonella symptoms include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps and typically occur 12 to 72 hours after eating contaminated food. It can cause serious and sometimes fatal infections in young children, the elderly, and people with weakened immune systems.

Salmonella outbreaks in the summer are fairly common, says Ellen Shumaker, a food safety expert at NC State Extension. People tend to eat more fresh produce in the summer and also dine outside more. “When we see warmer temperatures, that is going to create conditions that are favorable for bacteria like salmonella or parasites like cyclospora to grow,” she says. Food left unrefrigerated for more than two hours can be unsafe to eat.

But how does salmonella get into food in the first place? Unlike cyclospora, which only affects humans, salmonella can infect people and animals.

The egg recall involves a strain known as Salmonella enteritidis, which is known to affect poultry. It can colonize in the reproductive tract of laying hens and then be passed to eggs before the shell is formed. Laying hens can be exposed to salmonella through contaminated feed, water, or soil or through contact with infected wildlife or other animals. Humans can also bring the bacteria into laying facilities if it’s on their clothes or shoes.

“This specific type of salmonella has long been associated with eggs, and so this is a known issue,” says Jennifer McEntire, a food microbiologist and founder of the consulting firm Food Safety Strategy. The FDA requires egg producers with 3,000 or more laying hens to test for this type of salmonella.

When it comes to fresh produce, salmonella can be transmitted through contaminated irrigation water, which is also thought to be the most likely vehicle for spreading cyclospora.

Edward Dudley, a professor of food science at Penn State, says that in produce-growing regions that also have a lot of agriculture, there is always potential for waste from infected farm animals to come into contact with produce.

“The closer those two sites come to each other, the greater the chance that you're going to have salmonella or E. coli from the animals getting into surface waters that are used for irrigation that can eventually be transmitted to the crops,” he says.

He says people don’t need to be overly concerned about salmonella, especially if they’ve already thrown out the products affected by the recalls, “but certainly, be cautious.” That means washing your hands before handling food, cleaning food-prep and cooking surfaces, refrigerating perishables promptly, cooking foods to a safe internal temperature, and keeping raw meat, eggs, and poultry away from other foods in the kitchen.

“We have a technology right now to completely eliminate salmonella outbreaks, and it's called cooking,” he says. “But in the United States, we like eating fresh produce.”

Indeed, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has spent the summer encouraging people to do as much, when not touting a meat-and-ferments diet.

entries.summary: Tax season doesn’t have to be stressful. Score 10% off full service expert on federal tax filings and more exclusive TurboTax discount codes on WIRED.
entries.content:
TurboTax has been my go-to for self-filing taxes for years. It’s good enough for me—and literally millions of other users. TurboTax has quickly become a favorite among users for its easy-to-use self-filing services, along with easy access to assistance from tax professionals. TurboTax has free self-service for qualifying people, and TurboTax Live Assisted, where you file online with tax expert help if needed, and TurboTax Full Service, where a tax expert will do your taxes and review them with you before filing.

To help you figure out the often confusing process of filing taxes, I’ve written a guide on How to Pay Your Taxes Online, and The Best Tax Services. In both, I included TurboTax and similar services to help navigate between the options available for your specific tax needs. WIRED also has TurboTax coupons to save money while you begin the always-annoying task of filing your taxes this year. Canadian customers click here, these coupons are not for you.

Save 10% With TurboTax Service Codes and 2026 Early Filing Offers

Right now, you can get an extra 10% off Federal online tax filings with today’s TurboTax coupons. This price includes W-2 and 1040, with state returns for an additional fee. With ExpertFull Service, a tax professional will do your taxes for you, which costs a bit more than DIY-ing it, but can save you headaches and messes when it comes to what you owe. Things only get more expensive as tax season approaches, so file now to get the best price of the season.

If your taxes are a bit more straightforward, but you still have some questions, TurboTax Expert Assist (Live) offers the best of both worlds, where you file online yourself with tax expert help nearby if you end up needing it. With these TurboTax deals, you’ll get a 10% off TurboTax Live Assisted, with options starting at only $36 and (temporarily) capping out at $150 if you want to fully hand off your taxes. (Like the above service, this discount is for Federal tax products and filing early is the best way to ensure you’re getting the lowest price of the season).

*Price estimates are provided prior to a tax expert starting work on your taxes. Estimates are based on initial information you provide about your tax situation, including forms you upload to assist your expert in preparing your tax return and forms or schedules we think you’ll need to file based on what you tell us about your tax situation. Final price is determined at the time of print or electronic filing and may vary based on your actual tax situation, forms used to prepare your return, and forms or schedules included in your individual return. Prices are subject to change without notice and may impact your final price.

Give a 20% Off TurboTax Discount Code, Get up to $500

To save even more, get a TurboTax referral link, and when your friends use your link, they can get 20% off TurboTax federal products if they’re new customers of the service. As an added bonus, for each friend who files using your link, you’ll get a $25 gift card—you can earn up to a whopping $500 in gift cards (at this point, you’re basically getting another refund in gift cards). Here’s the nitty gritty: friends can receive 20% off the preparation and filing of federal tax return or business federal tax return through a TurboTax Online or TurboTax Live product, through October 31. You’ll get an email with the gift card or charitable donation within 45 days of your friend’s purchase. (Restrictions apply on TurboTax Free Edition, Intuit TurboTax Verified Pro, TurboTax State returns, TurboTax CD/Download products, and other add-on offerings.)

Save up to 20% on TurboTax Business Services

If you’re a small business owner, Expert Assist is probably the best service for you, with qualified tax experts at the ready to help you with any of those tricky filing questions. Right now, if you file your business tax returns with TurboTax, you’ll get 20% off one 2025 personal federal tax return. This type of service is best for those with S-corps and partnerships, and TurboTax will match you with a small business tax expert who knows your industry to maximize your deductions.

In addition to 20% off one personal tax filing offer for business customers, you can also get 10% off Business Expert Full Service and Expert Assist for small business owners. This discount applies to TurboTax federal products only (meaning no state products are included). These massive savings are in addition to early-season discounts.

File for $0 With TurboTax Free Edition

As mentioned above, users can file for free with TurboTax free edition. Around 37% of taxpayers qualify. Simple Form 1040 returns only (no schedules except for Earned Income Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit, Student Loan Interest, and Schedule 1-A). While this may not be the blanket service for every type of tax filer, this works for those with simple finances, so do a little research and see if TurboTax free edition may be right for you to save big instead of spending big. TurboTax free edition includes $0 to file for Federal taxes and $0 for State taxes. This service is ideal for simple uploads, like W-2’s, where all you’ll need to do is import, upload, or snap a photo of your W–2 and TurboTax will autofill your info for you, saving you time and potential headaches.

There are other ways to save too, with TurboTax discount codes for military members. As a thank you, military members can file their own taxes and get both their federal and state taxes done for free returns only (no schedules, except for EITC, CTC, student loan interest, and Schedule 1-A).

Other Free TurboTax Tools for Tax Season

In addition to the differing plans for individuals’ needs, TurboTax also has other helpful resources for this tax season, including a Tax Refund Calculator, where you can estimate your 2026 return by answering questions about your life and income. Similarly, TurboTax also offers a Tax Bracket Calculator to help you estimate your 2025 taxable income. All you need to do is enter your tax year filing status and taxable income to calculate your estimated tax rate.

With TurboTax, you start for free and pay only when you file—plus you get 100% accurate calculations, guaranteed. That’s not all with the guarantees either. TurboTax ensures a “Maximum Refund Guarantee,” meaning if you get a larger refund or less taxes due from another tax preparation method, they’ll refund the applicable TurboTax federal and/or state purchase price paid. You can also get quick answers for any tax questions from AI-Powered Intuit Assist, and for the lazy filers among us (myself included), you can upload or snap a photo of your W-2 and the info will be autofilled for you.

Is There a Service Code for TurboTax?

TurboTax service codes are unique codes, usually issued by customer support for specific situations; these will require you to input the code into the "I have a service code" field before payment. These single-use codes are for any technical or billing issues you may have during the tax filing process.

Even if you don’t have a service code, don’t fret—there are still tons of ways to get TurboTax coupons, including a discount of 10% when you file before Tax Day (April 15). Plus, you can get 20% off TurboTax referral codes if you use a friend’s invite link, and if you send your link to a friend and they purchase an online TurboTax product, you’ll receive e-gift cards of up to $500 as a reward from TurboTax. Save on federal and business tax filings by following here for limited-time offers throughout the 2026 tax season.

Contact a Local TurboTax Expert

If you have complicated taxes or just want that extra peace of mind this year, I’d recommend going with a local TurboTax expert to file your taxes for you. With this service, you’ll get matched with a tax expert who’s been matched to your unique tax situation starting at $129, which also includes W-2 and 1040 forms (state filing is an additional cost). Plus, you can connect online from the comfort of your home, or at a TurboTax store or Expert office near you.
